doc.title: Giacomo Gates interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 29, 2015 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Sitting in with Billy Mitchell at Sonny's Place
summary: At a Seaford jam session Billy Mitchell tested him on In Walked Bud and later sat in on his gig; Lou Donaldson also welcomed him.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Somebody asked him, they said, “I’d like to take a lesson with you in improvisation.” And Chet, who is a little salty sometimes, said, “well improvisation is about imagination or lack of it.” So I always remembered that. You’d better have something to say, otherwise don’t say much. Say a little then get out. A long, long time ago I went to a jam session at a club in Seaford, Long Island called Sonny’s Place. It was a club that was there for many years and many great players and singers stopped in there just to play for Sonny. And I called up to get a date there and Sonny said to me, “well come in on a Wednesday night, we have a jam session. If we like what you do we’ll give you a date.” So I show up and it’s a rhythm section and a tenor player. But the tenor player is Billy Mitchell of the Count Basie band. And this was probably mid or early 90s. Another guy who was not that fond of singers because he wanted to hear somebody who had something to say, or maybe even instrumentalists who had something to say. So I remember sitting down and the band plays the first set. And then they take a break and then they open it up. And there’s like four alto players and three tenor players lined up. And Billy Mitchell says on the microphone, I won’t use his expletives, but he said, “well I see we’ve got a lot of horn players tonight, so when you come up here, don’t play more than two choruses. Charlie Parker was a bad mickey-fickey, and he never played more than four.” So right away the horn players are putting their horns away now. You know? So I’m thinking wow, this is the real deal here. He’s not giving nobody no slack. So I finally get called up, and I get called up on the very last set because, well, “we’ll let the singer come up when it’s over.” He says, “well what do you got?” I said, “well could we do ‘In Walked Bud’?” He says, “yeah.” So I turned to the piano player. I said, “is F minor all right,” which is the standard key. And Billy says to me, “never mind what key it’s in, just sing it.” The bebop test. So I sing the song. And I scat a chorus and they play, and we take it out. And I turned to Billy Mitchell and I said, “Mr. Mitchell, thank you very much for letting me sit in with you. It was an honor.” And I go to walk away and he grabbed my shirt. He says, “wait a minute. As long as you’re up here you might as well sing

another one.” I said, “yes indeed.” So to be accepted by somebody who I looked up to, I wouldn’t have cared if he threw me off the bandstand. Because that’s what they do. But to be accepted like that is like just huge for me. I mean I drove home, it was like a two hour drive home, I’m going like, “wow, Billy Mitchell said it was okay.” And then I got a gig, about three months later. He [Sonny] gave me a date that night, for three months down the road. And I showed up with a rhythm section with guys that I knew from Long Island. And on the first set I see Billy Mitchell walk in with his horn. And on the break he said to me, “hey man, from the song” — and the second song I sang, I don’t know what it was, but I think it was something like “Confirmation” or something like that. He said to me, “from the songs that you sang when you sat in, I figured you’d have to bring a pretty good rhythm section. Do you mind if I sit in?” And I said, “do I mind if you sit in?” I said, “Mr. Mitchell, you put a chair on the bandstand and you stay as long as you like.” And he just smiled. “That’s right, baby.” Billy Mitchell sitting in? Come on. So that to me is worth a lot. You know? I mean I never had big representation or any of that other stuff. That made it happen. Lou Donaldson saying, “yeah man, come on up.” You know. “Yeah a friend of mine, come on up and sing a tune, Gates.”
Gates. Yeah you can’t buy that. That’s a great feeling to be accepted into that fraternity.
Of the hard core guys who don’t cut nobody no baloney.
It made me feel like it was all right.
